newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FOCUS - Taiwan trade, CPI data reaffirms money policy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Taiwan trade, CPI data reaffirms money policy.

text.p: Taiwan's steady January trade figures and lower-than-expected inflation will strengthen the central bank's resolve to maintain its loose monetary policy as a recovery slowly takes hold, experts said on Wednesday.
"Despite the stagnant trade growth, a well-expected result, we still foresee a slowly recovering domestic economy," said National Securities economist Lin Kuo-yang.

Recent indicators show that Taiwan's economy, which slowed dramatically in late 1995, began picking up in the fourth quarter of 1996, although analysts say the pace of recovery has been frustratingly slow despite a range of stimulatory measures.
Economists say they generally do not expect major changes in the trade picure in the first quarter of 1997 due to the high year-earlier comparative base, when exports and imports were peaking.
Taiwan posted a trade surplus of US$1.035 billion in January, down 0.6 percent from a surplus of US$1.041 billion in January 1996, the finance ministry announced on Wednesday.

January exports were US$10.326 billion, a decline of 3.4 percent year on year, while imports for the month were US$9.291 billion, down 3.7 percent year on year, it said. Both were the highest since February 1996.
The ministry noted that taking the 1.5 fewer work days in January into account, average daily exports and imports in fact rose 2.8 and 2.4 percent, respectively, from January 1996.
The January surplus was significantly bigger than an average forecast of US$822 million compiled from Tuesday's Reuters poll of Taiwan economists.
The exports figure was quite close to economists' forecast of US$10.308 billion, while imports were somewhat lower than their average forecast of US$9.486 billion.
Analysts have said that any bad news on the crucial export front could prompt the central bank to push for a Taiwan dollar depreciation, especially in light of the U.S. dollar's rise.

The Taiwan dollar slipped sharply in the final minutes of trade on Wednesday to end at T$27.508 to the U.S. dollar, taking its cue from a strong central bank hint late on Tuesday and an easing of pre-Lunar New Year holiday cash demand.

Wednesday brought good news on inflation. January's consumer price index, reported by the statistics directorate, rose 1.96 percent compared to January 1996 -- well below an average 3.18 percent forecast compiled from a Reuters poll on Monday.

Economists said the unexpectedly low CPI growth should ensure that the central bank adhered to its longstanding "stable to loose" monetary policy since the figure was well below the central bank's conservative 1997 CPI target of 3.31 percent.
"The low CPI growth should make the central bank feel comfortable and it should not tighten its monetary policy," said Nomura Securities economist Amy Huang.
However, economists cautioned that the central bank was unlikely to further loosen monetary policy for fear of fanning inflation or adding fuel to an already hot stock market.

The stock index has rallied 7.7 percent this year alone. The main index hit a six-year high of 7,346.88 points at the close on Monday, the last trading day before a seven-day Chinese new year holiday.

"The stock market has been overheating recently, with its rise far too liquidity-driven, so I don't expect the central bank to further loosen money policy despite such low CPI growth in January," said analyst Lin of National.
Economists surveyed for the Reuters poll had calculated that an average 9.0 percent rise in state-controlled oil prices on January 1 would add 0.387 percentage points to the CPI total.
Officials attributed the low CPI rise to low farm product prices and slowing service sector price increases, but cautioned that the oil price increase had not yet been fully reflected.
